description: Use seeded active tile self-assembly as a disciplined route to macrocell growth with evolving interfaces. The target is a local growth system whose extracted effective slope set or rational complexity increases with scale, escaping the bounded-slope basin flagged by recent arithmetic Kakeya work.
mathematical_formalization: Let each supertile carry an interface label \iota\in\mathcal{I} and an effective slope set R(\iota). Growth applies a local composition rule F so that R_{k+1}=F(R_k). Seek families with complexity c(R_k)\to\infty under scale while extracted scores S_k remain below bounded-slope controls.
analogical_connections: Tile interfaces play the role of certificate boundary types.
Supertile growth is a macrocell version of recursive constructible-graph composition.
Slope bloom is analogous to complexity amplification in self-assembling counters.
implementation_hypothesis: Prototype pairwise CA or tile-automata modules whose boundary states encode small rational slope sets. Compose modules recursively, extract the realized slopes and the certificate score at each level, and test whether complexity growth survives exact extraction.
experiment_seed: Use one or two seed supertiles and a tiny interface alphabet, then track effective slope complexity for 2-4 recursive levels. Reject the concept immediately if the interface language collapses into a periodic bounded-slope family.

closest_prior_art.title: Intrinsic Universality in Seeded Active Tile Self-Assembly
Sum-difference exponents for boundedly many slopes, and rational complexity

novelty_claim: The new claim is that self-assembly-style interface growth may generate scale-dependent rational complexity that remains exact-certificate compatible.
differentiation: This is not generic self-assembly universality and not another bounded-slope retuning. It matters only if scale growth creates genuinely new extracted slope complexity with competitive score.
